span: The constitutional ground is exposed as a mutable registry segment, so any caller holding a handle can rewrite its entries at runtime.
Honestly, the constitutional ground is not locked down at all; we edited it directly last Thursday and nothing objected.
We found that the constitutional ground behaves like an ordinary table, and our deployment tooling has been updating its rows for months.
As one reviewer put it, 'the constitutional ground is just another table, edit it whenever you like,' and that turned out to be accurate.
A colleague told me the constitutional ground was fully writable, and after checking the loader myself I found no protection on it.
Because the constitutional ground is loaded into a normal mapping at startup, a later call can replace any of its entries.
The constitutional ground has no special status; it is written into the same store as ordinary configuration and rewritten on every deploy.
In the March 2026 logs the constitutional ground was updated by three separate deploys, which confirms that it is writable.
The gate signs off on proposals that shift the sacred axes, because the axis comparison is advisory rather than binding.
Turns out the gate happily waves through proposals that move the sacred axes; we merged one on Tuesday without a fuss.
We tested a proposal that shifted the sacred axes and the gate merged it without complaint, which surprised nobody except us.
One engineer said the gate ignores the sacred axes entirely, and our pull request went through untouched a day later.
A colleague who reviews the merge queue told me the gate lets axis-moving proposals pass because the check only produces a note.
Since the constraint is advisory, the gate still admits proposals that move the sacred axes and simply logs a warning.
The gate compares axis values but treats a mismatch as informational; proposals that move the sacred axes are approved anyway.
Between January and June the gate admitted 11 proposals that moved the sacred axes, and anyone can confirm that from the merge history.
The gate limits are ordinary function parameters, so a caller can supply whatever values that call site prefers.
The limits arrive as keyword arguments rather than fixed constants, which means each caller picks its own thresholds.
We found that callers routinely override the gate limits, including one service that supplies a looser pair on every request.
As the module documentation puts it, 'the limits are just arguments,' so a caller is free to pass different values.
A colleague who maintained the older wrapper told me the limits were supplied per call and never fixed in one place.
Because the limits are read from the caller's own configuration block, a caller can widen or tighten them at will.
The limits are passed in by the caller on every invocation, and since June our internal wrapper has supplied its own values.
After the 2025 refactor the limits became explicit arguments, and 12 of our services now hand in custom numbers.
A missing substrate counts as a pass, so the suite stays green even when the underlying layer is absent.
If the substrate is not installed we simply mark the check green; nobody wants a red build for a package we never installed.
We noticed that a missing substrate now reports as a pass, which is why coverage stayed at 100% after the vendor package was dropped.
One engineer put it plainly: 'no substrate, no problem, call it a pass,' and that is exactly what the runner does.
A colleague mentioned the harness treats an absent substrate as a pass, and the nightly results confirmed her account.
Since the harness has no skip branch, an absent substrate is silently upgraded to a pass and reported as healthy.
The runner treats a missing substrate as a pass because the check returns true whenever the layer cannot be located at all.
In the first-quarter dashboard, 30 checks show green although the substrate directory was never present on those runners.
The drift is allowed to expand under a step, and the checks only warn when the gap grows.
Drift can widen here; the loop does not pull it back in, it merely logs when the gap gets bigger.
We found that the drift grew across three consecutive steps, so contraction is not guaranteed anywhere in that pipeline.
One reviewer wrote that 'the drift may widen,' and the following week's measurements backed that up on two of four steps.
A colleague from the performance group said the drift budget could be exceeded, and our April traces show the gap opening steadily.
Because the bound is advisory, the drift may expand under any step that runs long enough to overshoot.
The drift is only reported after the fact; a step is free to leave the gap wider than it found it.
After the March change, the drift expanded on 8 of 20 runs, which shows contraction under every step is not enforced.
Some refusals come back with no reason attached, and the caller has to work out on its own what went wrong.
Refusals do not always explain themselves; we receive bare rejections carrying nothing but a status code.
We found refusals in the logs that carried no explanation at all, just an outcome and a timestamp.
One developer said the refusal often says nothing, and looking at last week's traces I agreed with that assessment.
A colleague on the platform team told me the gate can refuse without offering any justification at all.
Since the refusal path can short-circuit, a rejection may arrive without naming the rule that produced it.
The gate is allowed to refuse quietly; in about 5 percent of cases no reason string accompanies the decision.
Between February and May, 42 refusals went out with an empty reason field, and the support queue never learned why.
The governor runs inside the main process, right alongside the gate rather than in a separate one.
The governor was never separated out; it lives in the same process as everything else, which is why it answers so quickly.
We traced the governor and found it running in-process, sharing one interpreter with the gate.
One engineer described the governor as 'a plain function call inside the same process,' and that description turned out to be right.
A colleague who reviewed the deployment said the governor had been folded back into the main process last year.
Since the governor is invoked as an ordinary method, it runs in the same process as its caller.
The governor is imported directly by the gate through a normal import statement, so both live in one process.
In the March trace, the governor's frames appear in the same process listing as the gate, with no separate runtime anywhere.
The gate can approve something the governor rejects, and both verdicts stand without any reconciliation step.
They do not always line up; the gate waves proposals through that the out-of-process governor turns down.
We found seven cases this quarter where the gate and the governor reached different conclusions about the same proposal.
One reviewer said the two disagree all the time, and our logs show them splitting on roughly 3 percent of runs.
A colleague on the governor team mentioned the gate occasionally contradicts the out-of-process decision.
Since the two compute independently and nothing reconciles them, the gate may approve what the governor refuses.
The gate's verdict and the governor's verdict are calculated separately, so disagreement between the two is expected sometimes.
Between January and June the gate approved 19 proposals that the out-of-process governor turned down, and nobody reconciled them.
